profile.name: Acrobatic Rock'n'Roll
profile.tagline: A high-speed, athletic competitive partner dance featuring rapid kicks and soaring acrobatics.
profile.insight: Dancers perform at such high intensity that a 90-second routine is physically equivalent to running an 800-meter race.
profile.profile: Acrobatic Rock'n'Roll is a competitive sports dance originating from Lindy Hop and Boogie Woogie traditions, regulated internationally by the World Rock'N'Roll Confederation. It features precise 6-basic and 9-basic kick-step footwork performed at fast tempos between 176 and 208 beats per minute. Competitors combine high-speed dancing with complex gymnastic elements like throws, lifts, and flips.
profile.profile_long:
Acrobatic Rock'n'Roll is a fast, athletic, physically demanding form of partner dance that originated from Lindy Hop but has evolved into a highly choreographed sport performed in formal competition. The history of the dance traces back to swing dance emerging around 1920 in the United States, which spawned Lindy Hop as the first partner dance to feature acrobatic elements. Around 1940, the style was modified for faster music to form Boogie-Woogie. With the rise of rock 'n' roll music in 1955, the dance underwent its final transformation into a competitive sport. In Europe, particularly in Lyon, France, during the late 1960s, local practitioners further codified and commercialized the style into what is now known as acrobatic rock, building a structured sporting discipline.

Technically, the dance is characterized by a rapid kick-step footwork style and impressive aerial maneuvers. The foundational movement relies on either a 6-basic step or the modern tournament 9-basic step featuring a kick-ball-change. Dancers execute sharp, linear kicks while moving almost exclusively on the balls of their feet. The World Rock'N'Roll Confederation (WRRC) regulates international competitions and enforces safety levels across various categories, ranging from youth divisions where acrobatics are prohibited to Main Class Free Style where advanced throws, lifts, and flips are performed. Because of its demanding technique, high speed, and acrobatics, it is a straining high-performance dance primarily performed by younger competitors.

Music for acrobatic rock and roll operates in a 4/4 measure. Unlike traditional rock 'n' roll music, the dance places stress on the first and third beats of each measure. Due to the high speed required—typically between 176 and 208 beats per minute (or 46 to 52 bars per minute)—traditional rock tracks have largely been replaced by modern disco and pop music. Costumes have similarly evolved from the original petticoats and jeans of the 1950s into multicoloured, form-fitting outfits made of elastic artificial fibres. These specialized garments provide the stretch and durability required to withstand the intense physical strain of lifts and throws while preventing friction injuries during acrobatics such as the Todessturz or the Einsteiger.

Organizationally, the sport is governed by national associations and the WRRC, which oversees World Cups, European championships, and World Championships. Notable figures in the history and practice of the sport include French pioneers and international competitors such as Miguel Angueira and Katerina Tikhonova. As the discipline continues to push athletic boundaries, it remains tightly codified to balance high-flying visual spectacle with strict safety regulations.

sections.origins_and_history: Acrobatic Rock'n'Roll emerged from swing dance traditions established around 1920 in the United States, evolving through Lindy Hop and Boogie-Woogie before crystallizing around 1955 alongside the music genre. In France, Lyon became a major incubator for the sport in the late 1960s, where local practitioners structured the dance into a commercial and competitive discipline.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced in pairs or groups, the form relies on precise 6-basic or 9-basic kick-ball-change footwork executed on the balls of the feet. Competitors alternate between rapid floor choreography and regulated acrobatic maneuvers, including lifts, jumps, throws, and flips.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is performed to a 4/4 measure at very fast tempos between 176 and 208 beats per minute (46 to 52 bars per minute), emphasizing the first and third beats. Modern tournaments favor high-tempo disco and pop music over traditional vintage recordings.
sections.costume_and_setting: Competitors wear form-fitting, multicoloured outfits made of elastic artificial fibres tailored individually to allow complete freedom of movement and prevent friction burns during acrobatics. Footwear includes light jazz shoes for dance segments and aerobics sneakers for shock absorption during aerial landings.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Acrobatic Rock'n'Roll is primarily performed in formal competitions, World Cups, and international championships regulated by the World Rock'N'Roll Confederation, functioning as a high-performance elite sports discipline.
sections.notable_figures: Notable figures associated with the sport include French world champion Miguel Angueira, Katerina Tikhonova, and early French developers such as Jacques Bense and Bernard Farhi.
sections.regional_variants: Specific rules, age categories, and allowed acrobatics vary by country and national association, though international standards are harmonized under WRRC safety levels.
sections.lineage: Derived from Lindy Hop and Boogie-Woogie, evolving directly into modern competitive acrobatic rock and roll.

teaching.rhythm: 4/4 measure with stress on the first and third beats
teaching.formation: Couples or groups (four to eight couples, or triples)
teaching.level_notes: Categories range from non-acrobatic Youth divisions to Main Class Free Style with advanced flips and throws.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Fast-paced offbeat phrasing with deliberate stress on the 1st and 3rd beats
music_profile.sound_description: Very fast modern pop and disco tracks with a heavy 4/4 driving rhythm, synthesized basslines, and punchy percussion designed to sustain rapid athletic movement.

movement_profile.posture: Upright, tightly controlled core, dancing almost exclusively on the balls of the feet
movement_profile.footwork: 6-basic and 9-basic kick-ball-change with sharp, linear kicks
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Active arm movements coordinated with leg kicks at clear, regular angles
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Body wave movements used to initiate partner lifts and throws
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Linear progression across the competition floor or stationary placement during acrobatics
movement_profile.partnering: Close contact during dance sequences transitioning into powerful throws, lifts, and catches
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Extremely rapid and snappy, between 176 and 208 bpm

signature_moves.name: Einsteiger
signature_moves.description: A sport variation where the lady springs off the man's hands to be catapulted into a high jump or flip.

signature_moves.name: Todessturz
signature_moves.description: An advanced high-level death drop acrobatic movement.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: No acrobatics in Youth class limited acrobatics in Juniors full free style flips in Main Class
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Unregulated acrobatics without safety protocols; landing without proper shock absorption.

activation_questions.question: What are the exact biomechanical shock loads experienced by female dancers during high-level landings?
activation_questions.why_needed: To optimize injury prevention protocols for joints and tibias.
activation_questions.next_evidence: WRRC medical committee injury study reports.
